content: Certainly. 1. For the treatment of abscesses, administer 15 mg/kg of the appropriate medication every 6 hours. For neonates and premature infants, refer to specific dosage and interval guidelines on page 70. Note that for interstitial pneumonia in children with HIV, administer 8 mg/kg of trimethoprim and 40 mg/kg of sulfamethoxazole three times daily for 21 days. Avoid co-trimoxazole in neonates who are premature or jaundiced. 2. For iron poisoning, administer deferoxamine at a dose of 15 mg/kg per hour intravenously, with a maximum of 80 mg/kg in 24 hours. Alternatively, administer intramuscularly at 50 mg/kg every 6 hours. 3. For neonatal seizures, phenobarbital is preferred over diazepam. Administer phenobarbital at 20 mg/kg intravenously or intramuscularly. If seizures persist, administer an additional 10 mg/kg intravenously or intramuscularly after 30 minutes. 4. For digoxin, calculate the exact dose based on the child’s body weight and the required infusion rate. Diluted solutions should be stored for no longer than 24 hours. Use 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose to prepare a solution of 1000 µg/mL. 5. For fentanyl, administer 1–4 µg/kg intravenously every 2–4 hours for pain relief. Alternatively, for continuous infusion, administer 0.5–1 µg/kg per hour, adjusting the dose based on the child’s weight and pain level. 6. For gentamicin, calculate the exact dose based on body weight. Avoid using undiluted 40 mg/mL gentamicin. For neonates and premature infants, refer to dosage guidelines on page 71. 7. For ketamine, used in major procedures requiring anesthesia, calculate the dose based on body weight. Administer 0.5–1 mg/kg. Refer to page 258 for detailed administration methods. 8. For mebendazole, administer 100 mg twice daily for 3 days for children older than 5 months. For giardiasis or amoebiasis, administer 10 mg/kg. 9. For morphine, calculate the dose based on the child’s weight. Administer 0.01 mg/kg per hour via intravenous infusion. 10. For quinine, administer a loading dose of 20 mg/kg of quinine hydrochloride salt intravenously over 2–4 hours after dilution in 10 mL/kg of IV fluid. The infusion rate should not exceed 5 mg/kg per hour. For oral administration, use quinine sulfate tablets, with the dose adjusted based on the child’s weight. 11. For vitamin A supplementation, administer once daily for 2 days. Use 200,000 IU capsules for older children and adjust the dose for younger children as per weight and age. 12. For neonatal resuscitation, initiate positive pressure ventilation with air for infants with a gestational age greater than 32 weeks. For very preterm infants, start with 30% oxygen if available. Ensure the infant is warm, dry, and positioned correctly. Begin ventilation with a mask and self-inflating bag within 1 minute of birth if the infant is not breathing or gasping. 13. For severe malnutrition, assess for emergency signs such as lethargy, sunken eyes, or inability to drink. If present, administer IV glucose and fluids as per guidelines. If the child is not lethargic or unconscious, provide glucose orally or via a nasogastric tube. 14. For severe dehydration in children with diarrhea, assess for signs such as lethargy, sunken eyes, and very slow skin pinch. Administer rehydration fluids as per the hospital’s treatment plan. 15. For antimicrobial treatment of common conditions, refer to your country’s updated treatment guidelines. For example: Dysentery: Administer the recommended antibiotic as per local guidelines. Severe malaria: Administer the appropriate antimalarial drug intravenously, following the dosage guidelines. Severe pneumonia: Administer antibiotics intravenously, adjusting the dose based on the child’s weight. 16. For intravenous fluids in neonates, infants, and children, use solutions containing appropriate sodium and glucose concentrations to prevent hyponatremia and hypoglycemia. Avoid using solutions with very low sodium content for rehydration or maintenance. 17. For nutritional assessment, calculate the child’s weight-for-age or weight-for-height using standardized growth charts. Identify malnutrition based on deviations from the median values, with -2 SD indicating low weight-for-age and -3 SD indicating very low weight-for-age. 18. For emergency care, manage airway obstructions, provide oxygen, and ensure the child is warm. Insert an IV line for fluid administration if necessary. For children with trauma or surgical conditions, seek surgical consultation or follow surgical guidelines. 19. For daily monitoring in hospitalized children, record vital signs, fluid balance, treatments administered, and nutritional intake. Adjust treatment plans based on the child’s progress and clinical condition. This version provides clear, professional, and detailed instructions suitable for medical professionals.
